Developer Docs

# **Ramp MCP**

---

Ramp MCP connects AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor to your Ramp account. Each connection acts as the signed-in user, with that user's Ramp permissions.

## Connect

* **Claude:** Install Ramp from Claude's directory, then sign in to Ramp.
* **ChatGPT:** Install Ramp from the ChatGPT app directory.
* **Cursor:** Add Ramp to Cursor with one click.
* **Claude Code:**

```
claude mcp add --transport http ramp https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

  

* **Codex:**

```
codex mcp add ramp --url https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

  

* **Other clients:** Coding agents can also use Ramp CLI. For other MCP clients, gateways, and the sandbox, see Connect to Ramp.

When you sign in, choose **Full access** or **Read-only**. Connections expire after 30 days; reconnect to renew.

## Connection issues

* **"The app you are using is not currently supported"** means your client's redirect URI isn't allowlisted. Request a redirect URI.
* **You can't connect at all:** your Ramp role may not include access to AI tools. Ask your Admin; see Manage connected AI tools.

For the full tool list and more troubleshooting, see Connect to Ramp and the Agent tools reference.

Guides

# Connecting

There are three ways to connect your agents to Ramp:

MCP, CLI, and API connection options

| Criterion | CLI | MCP Connectors | API |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Set up | Instant | Instant to 15 minutes | Hours to days |
| How it runs | In a terminal, local agent, script, or CI | Inside a conversational assistant | In deterministic code |
| Permission and Attribution | Actions are attributed to the acting user or agent. The agent acts as the Ramp user who authenticated the connection. Permissions do not exceed the user or agent's role. | Actions are attributed to the acting user or agent. The agent acts as the Ramp user who authenticated the connection. Permissions do not exceed the user or agent's role. | Access is limited to the scopes granted to your app. |
| Strengths | Structured output, broad workflows, and easy local automation | Easy setup, already available in some cases, and instant with Claude chat or an out-of-the-box connector | Maximum control over interfaces, workflows, and backend logic |
| Weaknesses | Requires installation and access to a coding agent or terminal | Slower performance | Requires the most engineering, security, and lifecycle ownership |

Use the Ramp app when a person needs to review context,
handle an exception, or complete work directly. The
Agent Tools reference lists every tool available
in the CLI and MCP.

## CLI

Use the CLI when the agent has terminal access, needs structured output, or
should follow a repeatable skill. The CLI works well in Claude Code, Codex,
Cursor, scripts, and CI.

## Connect via MCP

Choose the client you already use. Each link opens the fastest available way to
add Ramp.

### Coding agents

```
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http ramp https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
 
# Codex
codex mcp add ramp --url https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

Coding agents can also use the CLI.

## What the connection can do

The connection acts as the Ramp user who authorized it and never exceeds that
user's permissions. On the consent screen, the user chooses **Full access** or
**Read-only**. Connections expire after 30 days; reconnect to renew. Admins
control who can connect with the **Manage connections to Ramp via MCP, CLI and
other AI connectors** role permission and can revoke connections; revoking one
cuts off every AI tool that shares it. See
Manage connected AI tools.

## Developer API

Use the API when your product owns the interface and backend workflow. Your
team is responsible for OAuth, scopes, webhooks, retries, and the customer
experience.

View API reference

## Custom MCP clients

Point the client at `https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp`. For the Ramp sandbox
(demo.ramp.com, the same environment as the CLI's `--env sandbox`), use
`https://demo-mcp.ramp.com/mcp`. Clients that read MCP JSON usually expect:

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ramp": {
      "url": "https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

Custom clients and gateways need their exact redirect URI allowlisted before
authorization can complete:

* Use `https://`, or `http://` only with `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`. Ramp also
  accepts the `claude://`, `cursor://`, `grokbot://`, and `perplexity-app://`
  schemes; other custom schemes are not supported.
* Submit the exact host. Wildcard subdomains are not supported.
* Request redirect URI access
  for the client or gateway.

## Troubleshooting

### Authentication stops working

Connections expire after 30 days. Disconnect and reconnect Ramp in the client to
renew. If a custom client keeps stale credentials, clear its cached MCP auth.

### Write tools are missing

The connection may be read-only. Reconnect and choose **Full access**, and
check that the user's Ramp role allows the action.

### The CLI keeps logging out

CLI sessions stay signed in while they are used and refresh on each use. After
a period of inactivity, run `ramp auth login` again. If it happens sooner,
confirm that the runtime preserves `~/.config/ramp/config.toml`; ephemeral
coding environments may replace that file between sessions.

### A query returns too much data

Reporting queries return up to 1,000 rows per page. Narrow the date range or
filters, or ask the agent to page through the results.

### Unsupported redirect URI

See Custom MCP clients to submit the exact URI.

### A receipt attachment does not reach MCP

Chat attachments are not forwarded to Ramp MCP. Ask the agent for a receipt
upload link, or use the Ramp CLI or Ramp app.

# Ramp MCP overview

## Overview

Ramp MCP connects Ramp to AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor. From those tools, you can review spend, look up bills and vendors, and handle approvals and expenses. A connected tool can only see and do what your Ramp role allows, and Ramp attributes its actions to you.

## Connect an AI tool

You need a Ramp account and access to the AI tool. Most Ramp roles can connect by default. If you can't, ask your Admin; see Manage connected AI tools.

* Claude: Install Ramp from Claude's MCP directory, then sign in to Ramp.
* ChatGPT: Install Ramp from the ChatGPT app directory.
* Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor: Connect with Ramp MCP or the Ramp CLI. See Connect Ramp to an agent.
* Other AI tools: Any tool that supports remote MCP servers with OAuth can connect to

  ```
  https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
  ```

  . See For developers for custom clients.

When you sign in, choose Full access to let the tool make changes, or Read-only to let it view data only. Your Ramp permissions apply either way.

Connections expire after 30 days. To renew one, reconnect from your AI tool.

## What you can do with Ramp

Ask in plain language. Some examples:

| Area | Try asking |
| --- | --- |
| Spend analysis | "Show me our top software vendors by spend this quarter." |
| Bills | "Find our open bills from AWS and when they're due." |
| Approvals | "Summarize the bills and reimbursements waiting on my approval and flag anything unusual." |
| Expenses | "Find my draft lunch reimbursement from Tuesday and tell me what is missing." |
| Receipts and memos | "Which of my transactions from the last 14 days are missing receipts or memos?" |
| Receipt upload | "Upload the receipt for my Uber ride last Tuesday." |
| Policy and help | "Is my planned $300 client dinner within policy?" |
| Cards and funds | "Lock my card — I can't find it." |
| Procurement | "Submit a procurement request for 20 Figma seats." |
| Travel | "Show my upcoming flights and hotels for next month." |
| Ramp Banking | "Get all Ramp Banking account balances for today's cash snapshot." |

For every available tool, see the Ramp agent tools reference. Some tools aren't available to every business.

> Important: If you're an approver, the AI tool can approve or reject transactions, reimbursements, bills, and requests on your behalf. Approving a bill can send it to payment.

## For developers

* Coding agents, the Ramp CLI, and custom MCP clients: See the Ramp agent docs.
* Custom clients and MCP gateways such as Glean, MintMCP, or Microsoft Copilot Studio: Ramp must allowlist the redirect URI first. Submit a redirect URI allowlist request.
* Custom integrations: Use the Ramp Developer API.

For other questions, ask your AI tool to "submit feedback to Ramp," or see How to contact Ramp's Support team.

# Building Ramp's MCP server

Junho Choi

We built a `Ramp MCP` server that lets you interact with your business data using natural language—by turning our developer API into a SQL interface that an LLM can query.

We asked Claude to “give me a detailed overview of my business’s spend in the past year.” The results were mind-blowing

## What MCP is and how we used it

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard developed by Anthropic that enables applications to expose data and functionality to LLMs. MCP provides an LLM with access to pretty much anything you want: databases, your computer’s filesystem, Figma, GitHub, etc. Given that Ramp’s developer API is the primary way to access Ramp’s resources externally, we wanted to see what would happen if we put the two together.

An MCP server in Python can be built using `FastMCP`. MCP "tools" are akin to HTTP endpoints the LLM can access through an MCP client. The following piece of code, for example, is reminiscent of a `Flask` HTTP endpoint decorated with `@app.route(…)` and OpenAPI spec schemas.

```
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("My MCP")

@mcp.tool(…) # tool name or function name used to annotate tool name
async def my_tool(
	param_1: str, # params and their type hints are parsed to annotate the tool input schema
	param_2: list[int],
	param_3: Optional[dict[str, Any]] = None,
	...
) -> str:
	"""
	Docstring is parsed to annotate the tool description
	"""
	results = await some_api(...) # expose your filesystem, some REST API, DB, etc.
	return f"Do something with these results: {'\n'.join(results)}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
	mcp.run(transport='stdio') # available with stdio or SSE transport
```

Using `FastMCP` and a lightweight Ramp developer API client, we were able to build a working early prototype of the Ramp MCP server. With Claude Desktop as our MCP client, Claude was able to both generate visualizations and run simple analyses on spend data pulled from Ramp’s APIs using natural language. Adding a new source of data *— like a different API endpoint —* was as simple as defining a new tool. As a proof of concept, we had it issue cards on demand for a company offsite.

## LLMs are surprisingly good at SQL

Our initial setup worked fine on a small demo business, but we quickly ran into a few scaling issues: miscalculations, limited context windows, input size limits, and high input token usage. At first we hacked together a simple pagination tool to chunk responses into smaller, digestible parts, but we struggled to scale meaningfully beyond a few hundred transactions. Then we asked Claude what it would prefer the data to look like, and it said it preferred predictable data formats that enabled server-side functions. That sounded like SQL: structured, predictable, and built for querying. Most importantly, Claude could now load as little raw data into its context window as possible, making the server do most of the heavy computational lifting. Thanks to the reduced token usage in this approach, Ramp MCP now even worked with the free version of Claude.

Everything aside from Developer API is running locally

In order to implement a SQL interface to analyze our API data, we built a lightweight in-memory ETL that pulls data from our APIs, transforms it, and loads it into an in-memory SQLite database.

To transform our RESTful API’s JSON responses into SQL rows, we flattened the JSON and inferred the appropriate SQL column type based on the value types. To keep things simple, we set missing keys as `NULL` and cast lists to text.

```
{"id": 10, "amount": 123, "user": {"id": 1, "cardholder_first_name": "Eric"}}
```

becomes

```
id      | user_cardholder_first_name | user_id | amount
10      | "Eric"                     | 1       | 123
```

Reporting use cases involve a ton of data and complex queries, often leading to timeouts. As a solve, we added an interface to an OLAP-powered API built by our data platform team. This allowed us to extract spend data which was specifically optimized for reporting use cases, solving the timeouts.

To expose all of this functionality to the LLM, we defined a few different tools:

1. Several “load” tools (e.g. `load_transactions`) to pull data from the Ramp API
2. A `process_data` tool to transform the data from the API and load into the SQLite table (we could've skipped this step to reduce roundtrips)
3. An `execute_query` to run queries on the in-memory database directly

After this move to a SQL-based paradigm, Claude went from struggling with a few hundred data points to accurately analyzing tens of thousands of spend events. It can now load as little or as much data as it needs while running aggregate or window functions to gain a better understanding of the data. With these changes, the latency for extracting data from the API became the largest bottleneck as tool calls started timing out.

Claude querying Ramp spend data from an in-memory SQLite database

LLMs are significantly better at SQL than at math, which is why this set of tools made sense for our RESTful API to expose relational spend data effectively. MCP allows you to create whatever interface works best for the type of data you want to connect to it, and it's on you to tinker a bit to figure out what the best data access strategy is.

## Where Ramp MCP shines (and where it breaks down)

Our open-source `ramp-mcp` server can access a business context using a variety of tools, and enable natural language access to your Ramp data. It can create curated views of your spend, identify potential cost savings, and help you navigate your business hierarchy *— all while surfacing insights we hadn’t even considered.*

There are still limitations. There's the occasional reliability issue, and API latency can be high for very large businesses with a lot of data. There are plenty of optimizations we could implement (concurrent requests, pulling data from the APIs asynchronously, smart caching, using DuckDB, etc.), but building a scalable, and truly reliable agentic AI requires a great deal of complex technical work beyond what MCP currently offers. Write tools can be particularly unreliable, so we'll work on a safety framework before releasing tools that can perform actions in your business on your behalf as an agentic LLM.

## Ramp MCP and Audit Logs

MCP and similar technologies can introduce information security risk if left unchecked. LLMs can pull and understand large amounts of data from any source at their disposal. This means authentication credentials like API keys need to be secured, and following the principle of least privilege is as crucial as ever. As a mitigant, we implemented audit logging and you can pick a constrained set of OAuth scopes and tools to make available to the MCP client.

Audit logs for the Ramp developer API

Keep in mind that LLMs themselves may not always pick the correct tools, or they may use them incorrectly. Prompt engineering may alleviate some of this issue, but in our testing Claude occasionally made mistakes even when given the same prompt twice across separate conversations.

## Conclusions

MCP is early, with many limitations to overcome, and also a strong and growing community of engineers that can see the tip of the iceberg for how transformative this technology can be. Many MCP servers have been made available by businesses and enthusiasts alike, and anyone can connect their MCP client to a wide range of tools in their tech stack.

Client or server, I encourage you to give it a try. Miss out at your own peril!
